extracted.intended_audience: college-level journalism educators and news-writing instructors (visual communication faculty)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and using a videotaped mock press conference to teach news-writing students how to prepare for, cover, and critique press conferences. Includes production, pedagogy, student preparation, and evaluation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researching questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should research the questions to be asked at the press conference, delving into a wide array of topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example topics used: airport expansion/relocation, sewerage system problems, mass transit plans, solid waste management, library development, traffic/growth issues, earthquake preparedness, city elections, image of politicians. Research helps formulate substantive, newsworthy questions and avoid superficial queries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press conference etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach and observe press conference etiquette such as standing when asking questions, note taking, and general decorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student criticism noted: 'The students should have stood up when they spoke.' Instructors can model etiquette and pause tape to point out correct/incorrect behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to ask relevant and logical follow-up questions that extract specifics and advance the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: failing to ask for names or specifics (e.g., not asking McCarty to name the 'politically unsophisticated' candidates) — missed opportunity for 'tantalizing news copy.' Praise given where a follow-up about stadium checks post-earthquake was called 'a good one.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical sequencing of questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions should follow a logical sequence and group related topics rather than jumping back and forth unpredictably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem noted: students asked about recycling, then stadium/library, then returned to recycling — reviewers commented students did not always ask follow-ups in a logical sequence. Use tape to highlight sequencing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'light' questions to warm sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate lighter, rapport-building questions designed to get the subject to 'warm up' to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: asking about the deputy mayor's family as a 'light' question; it generated a lively, candid response. Use balanced mix of light and substantive questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question phrasing for live/broadcast settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame questions so they cut through 'garbage' and enable reporters to get answers in fast-paced, live settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student comment: in live press conferences reporters have to be aggressive and 'word their questions in such a manner that they can get past all the garbage.' Emphasize brevity and clarity for broadcast-style questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with cooperative and uncooperative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Train students on techniques for handling both cooperative and uncooperative interviewees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students discussed strategies in preparation; future video idea: produce a mock press conference with an uncooperative source to test responses and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note-taking skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize effective note taking during the conference so reporters can accurately capture quotes, facts, and follow-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among preparation topics; instructors can pause tape to point out good/bad note-taking behavior and its impact on subsequent reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of the press conference (press corps vs source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach who controls the flow of a press conference and methods reporters can use to assert control or recover the agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the videotape to discuss 'who controls the press conference — the press corps or the source?' Offer examples of techniques for steering or reclaiming the exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism of production/set design
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a realistic set (podium, press seating, photographer, lighting) and use an actual public figure when possible to simulate real conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producer arranged podium and press-conference-like seating and brought a photographer; students noted realism because McCarty was an actual public figure. Suggestion: add a table in front of experts during evaluation segment (student critique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an actual public figure vs actor
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a real public official enhances realism and learning value compared to using an actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student comment: 'The fact that Judy McCarty is an actual public figure and not an actress made the press conference that much more realistic and interesting.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation/critique segment by professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a professional evaluation segment (journalist and broadcast professor) to review performance and point out strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The videotape included an 18-minute evaluation by a staff writer and a broadcast journalism professor; students found the critique 'as valuable as the press conference itself.' Recommendation: reviewers should show both mistakes and things students did right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance praise and criticism in critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques should highlight good performance as well as mistakes to reinforce positive behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student suggestion: 'The reviewers should have shown more of the things that students did right rather than focusing on their mistakes.' Use taped examples of positives for modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pause-and-discuss pedagogical use of videotape
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the videotape's pausing capability to stop at teachable moments and discuss techniques, phrasing, and approaches while fresh in students' minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical advantage: playing back on a VCR permits the instructor to stop the conference at any point to point out good or bad things; allows immediate discussion of phrasing and approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing to create short exemplars for immediate comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Edit the tape to extract short good/bad question examples so reviewers can comment immediately rather than waiting for the conference to finish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future idea: film editing to allow quick discussion of good and bad examples, enabling immediate reviewer feedback rather than delayed critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the tape as a prelude to real coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the mock press conference as a preparatory exercise before assigning students to conduct or critique real press conferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tape is a good preliminary to having students do a press conference on their own and to watching/critique nationally televised press conferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging active participation and 'learning by doing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize experiential learning — participation and being 'on the spot' — over lecture to build practical skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student comments: 'The best thing about the press conference is that it offered participation and experience' and 'it is always better to learn by doing.' The mock event forces students to think on their feet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability for repeated viewing/out-of-class study
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the tape available for students to view multiple times outside of class to increase time on task and reinforce learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated viewing allows students who need more practice to watch again; videotape can be loaned or shown outside class for reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness of producing teaching videotape
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider production costs and feasibility — minimal expense can produce effective instructional materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tape was produced with a $400 grant (much went to studio rental). Not commercially available but inexpensive to produce for instructional use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic selection for enduring relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose subject matter that remains relevant over time so the tape can be reused (issues that are 'relatively timeless').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: earthquake preparedness, sewerage systems, landfill issues, traffic and growth — these issues will persist and keep the tape useful across semesters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating emotional and nonverbal cues via visual media
rubrics_metrics.description: Use video to capture participants' emotions, exact words, and facial/body cues that are not easily captured in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student observation: tape shows participants and their emotions and expressions — 'things that can't be as easily captured on paper' — making visual communication especially valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation protocol for subject (not telling questions in advance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not inform the interviewed subject of specific questions beforehand to simulate authentic press-conference conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this production Judy McCarty was not told in advance what questions to expect, creating more spontaneous and realistic interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the tape as a writing exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign students to cover the mock press conference as if it were real to practice news-writing and story development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The videotaped press conference can serve as a writing exercise where students produce news copy from the mock event, allowing assessment of reporting and writing skills.
